def register(cls: type[AttentionMethod]) -> type[AttentionMethod]:
    """Class decorator: add ``cls`` to the bank under ``cls.name``.

    Raises ``KeyError`` on a duplicate name, so two methods can never silently shadow
    each other.  Registration is all it takes to be picked up by the conformance
    suite -- there is no second list to update.

    Examples
    --------
    >>> import attnbank as ab
    >>> @ab.register                                     # doctest: +SKIP
    ... class MyAttention(ab.AttentionMethod):
    ...     name = "mine"
    ...     category = ab.Category.RESTRICT
    """
    if cls.name in _REGISTRY and _REGISTRY[cls.name] is not cls:
        raise KeyError(f"duplicate method name: {cls.name}")
    _REGISTRY[cls.name] = cls
    return cls

docs.title: backends
docs.text:
Execution backends: what actually runs, whether it is here, and what it would cost.

A method in this bank is two things that are easy to confuse: an operator (the mathematics, one file, written for clarity) and an execution path (how that operator is evaluated). The operator never changes with the backend. The execution path does.

import attnbank as ab

print(ab.backends())                          # what this machine can run, and why not
ab.build("softmax", backend="sdpa")           # ask for one explicitly
ab.backend_matrix()                           # which method supports which

Four backends are known to the library:

reference Plain PyTorch, always available, CPU and CUDA, every dtype. It is the correctness anchor: every other backend is tested against it, so it is also the default. Slow on purpose -- DESIGN.md Sec. 6 asks these implementations to be readable. sdpa torch.nn.functional.scaled_dot_product_attention. No extra dependency, and on CUDA it dispatches to FlashAttention-2 or the memory-efficient kernel; pass sdpa_kernel="flash" | "mem_efficient" | "math" to pin the sub-backend instead of letting torch choose. flash_attn The flash-attn package (Dao et al.). CUDA only, fp16/bf16 only. xformers / triton Detected and reported, but no method declares them. For xformers the reason is that sdpa already routes to the same memory-efficient kernel in torch >= 2.2; for triton, that the bank ships no hand-written kernel. ab.backends() says so rather than leaving you to guess.

Declaring a backend is a claim that it equals the reference, and tests/test_conformance.py::test_backend_equivalence is where that claim is checked -- for every method, every declared backend, both causal settings, fp32 and fp64, plus the awkward shapes. A method whose output is not literally a dense softmax over a mask, or whose extras need the full score matrix anyway, declares reference only. That is the right answer for most of the bank, and it is stated rather than implied.

Examples:

>>> import attnbank as ab
>>> ab.get_default_backend()
'reference'
>>> ab.is_backend_available("reference")
True
>>> ab.get_class("softmax").backends
('reference', 'sdpa', 'flash_attn')
>>> ab.get_class("nmf_oracle").backends
('reference',)

def set_default_backend(name: str) -> str:
    """Set the process-wide default backend; returns the previous one.

    The studies behind the monograph pin this to ``'reference'`` on import
    (``attnbank/studies/__init__.py``) so that adding a backend can never move a
    published number.

    Examples
    --------
    >>> import attnbank as ab
    >>> previous = ab.set_default_backend("sdpa")
    >>> ab.get_default_backend()
    'sdpa'
    >>> ab.set_default_backend(previous)
    'sdpa'
    """
    global _DEFAULT
    if name not in DISPATCHABLE:
        raise BackendNotSupportedError(
            f"{name!r} cannot be a default backend. Dispatchable backends are: "
            f"{', '.join(DISPATCHABLE)}. ab.backends() explains the others.")
    if not is_backend_available(name):
        info = backend_info(name)
        raise BackendNotSupportedError(
            f"{name!r} is not available here: {info.reason}."
            + (f" Fix: {info.install}" if info.install else ""))
    previous, _DEFAULT = _DEFAULT, name
    return previous

resolve_backend(
    requested: Optional[str],
    supported: Sequence[str],
    method: str,

Pick the backend to run, loudly.

  • requested is None -- use the process default if the method supports it and it is installed, otherwise reference. Falling back from the default is quiet, because the default is a preference, not an instruction.
  • requested is not declared by the method -- raise BackendNotSupportedError listing what it does declare. An explicit request is an instruction; silently doing something else would make a benchmark meaningless.
  • requested is declared but not installed here -- warn with BackendFallbackWarning and use reference. Announced, never silent.

Examples:

>>> from attnbank.backends import resolve_backend
>>> resolve_backend(None, ("reference", "sdpa"), "softmax")
'reference'
>>> resolve_backend("sdpa", ("reference", "sdpa"), "softmax")
'sdpa'
>>> resolve_backend("sdpa", ("reference",), "nmf_oracle")

attnbank.backends.BackendNotSupportedError: 'nmf_oracle' does not support backend 'sdpa'...
Source code in attnbank/backends.py 
def resolve_backend(requested: Optional[str], supported: Sequence[str],
                    method: str) -> str:
    """Pick the backend to run, loudly.

    * ``requested is None`` -- use the process default if the method supports it and it
      is installed, otherwise ``reference``. Falling back from the *default* is quiet,
      because the default is a preference, not an instruction.
    * ``requested`` is not declared by the method -- raise
      :class:`BackendNotSupportedError` listing what it does declare. An explicit
      request is an instruction; silently doing something else would make a benchmark
      meaningless.
    * ``requested`` is declared but not installed here -- warn with
      :class:`BackendFallbackWarning` and use ``reference``. Announced, never silent.

    Examples
    --------
    >>> from attnbank.backends import resolve_backend
    >>> resolve_backend(None, ("reference", "sdpa"), "softmax")
    'reference'
    >>> resolve_backend("sdpa", ("reference", "sdpa"), "softmax")
    'sdpa'
    >>> resolve_backend("sdpa", ("reference",), "nmf_oracle")
    Traceback (most recent call last):
        ...
    attnbank.backends.BackendNotSupportedError: 'nmf_oracle' does not support backend 'sdpa'...
    """
    supported = tuple(supported)
    if requested is None:
        wanted = get_default_backend()
        if wanted in supported and is_backend_available(wanted):
            return wanted
        return REFERENCE
    if requested not in supported:
        extra = ""
        if requested in _DETECTORS and requested not in DISPATCHABLE:
            extra = f" {backend_info(requested).reason.capitalize()}."
        elif requested not in _DETECTORS:
            extra = f" Known backends: {', '.join(sorted(_DETECTORS))}."
        raise BackendNotSupportedError(
            f"{method!r} does not support backend {requested!r}. It declares: "
            f"{', '.join(repr(b) for b in supported)}.{extra} "
            "ab.backend_matrix() shows the whole matrix; a method that declares "
            "'reference' only has no equivalent kernel, which is a fact about the "
            "operator, not a gap in the library.")
    if not is_backend_available(requested):
        info = backend_info(requested)
        warnings.warn(
            f"backend {requested!r} was requested for {method!r} but is not available "
            f"here ({info.reason}); falling back to {REFERENCE!r}. "
            + (f"Fix: {info.install}. " if info.install else "")
            + "This is announced because a silent downgrade would make a benchmark "
              "meaningless.",
            BackendFallbackWarning, stacklevel=3)
        return REFERENCE
    return requested

@classmethod
def from_class(cls, klass: type[AttentionMethod]) -> "MethodInfo":
    """Read the declaration attributes and ``__init__`` signature off a class."""
    conv = klass.convergence_configs()
    params: dict[str, Any] = {}
    try:
        sig = _inspect.signature(klass.__init__)
    except (TypeError, ValueError):  # pragma: no cover - builtins
        sig = None
    if sig is not None:
        for pname, p in sig.parameters.items():
            if pname in ("self", "kw", "kwargs") or p.kind is p.VAR_KEYWORD:
                continue
            params[pname] = (None if p.default is p.empty else p.default)
    return cls(
        name=klass.name,
        class_name=klass.__name__,
        category=klass.category.value,
        objective=klass.objective.value,
        supports_causal=bool(klass.supports_causal),
        expresses_weights=bool(klass.expresses_weights),
        row_stochastic=bool(klass.row_stochastic),
        head_independent=bool(klass.head_independent),
        trainable=bool(klass.trainable),
        references=tuple(klass.references),
        paper_section=klass.paper_section,
        backends=tuple(klass.backends),
        limit_config=klass.limit_config(),
        n_convergence_configs=0 if conv is None else len(conv),
        summary=_summary(klass),
        parameters=params,
        doc=_inspect.getdoc(klass) or "",
    )

docs.title: Examples gallery
docs.text:
Short, self-contained scripts. Every one of them runs as written, and tests/test_examples.py executes all of them in CI, so a broken example is a failing build rather than a stale page.

git clone https://github.com/Ashkan13776/attnbank
python attnbank/examples/01_quickstart.py
example what it shows 1 Quickstart: one import, three calls The whole library behind one name. attend for the one-liner, build for the object you keep, compare for the numbers you report. 2 Invariant W: every method is a measure times a value field y == weights @ (v_hat if v_hat is not None else value) holds for every registered method -- that is the claim the library is built on, and here it is, checked over the whole bank in float64. 3 Splitting output error into its two causes An approximation can be wrong in two ways: it attends to the wrong places, or it aggregates the wrong values. metrics.error_decomposition separates them exactly: text y - y_hat = (pi - pi_hat) v + pi_hat (v - v_hat) \_____________/ \________________/ distributional value 4 Top-k is not output-optimal Selecting the k largest attention weights minimises the omitted mass eps_q = pi_q(S^c). It does not minimise ||y - y_hat||, because the bound is eps_q * osc(v) and a light token carrying an extreme value can matter more than a heavy token sitting near the mean. 5 Random features: the error that shrinks, and the error that does not FAVOR+ (performer) estimates exp(<q, k>) with r positive random features. More features, less error -- and the conformance suite checks that this is monotone, because for a Monte-Carlo method "reduces to softmax at some finite setting" is not available as a correctness anchor. 6 Attention-matrix error is not output error Most of the literature reports ||P - P_hat||_F. The quantity a model actually feels is ||(P - P_hat) V||. They are not the same ranking: the Frobenius norm charges a method for mass it moved between two tokens with nearly identical values, which costs the output nothing. 7 Finding your way around the bank Thirty-odd methods is too many to remember and too few to need a search engine. Four calls cover it: categories for the taxonomy, list_methods for the table, available for the names, describe for one method in full. 8 What a method actually saves Every method declares an analytic cost model: flops, state_bytes (the resident KV cache) and bytes_moved. Decoding is bandwidth-bound, so bytes_moved -- not flops -- is the number that predicts latency, and state_bytes is the number that decides whether the context fits at all. 9 Adding a method: declare, implement, conform Three steps. Subclass attnbank.AttentionMethod, declare what the method is, implement _forward. The declaration is not documentation -- the conformance suite reads it and tests the method against it, so a wrong declaration is a failing build. 10 Backends: the operator stays, the execution path changes A method is two things: an operator (the mathematics, one readable file) and an execution path. The operator never changes with the backend -- and that is a tested claim, not a slogan.

examples/01_quickstart.py
"""
Quickstart: one import, three calls
===================================

The whole library behind one name. ``attend`` for the one-liner, ``build`` for the
object you keep, ``compare`` for the numbers you report.
"""
import torch

import attnbank as ab

torch.manual_seed(0)

# [B, H, m, d] queries against [B, H, n, d] keys and [B, H, n, dv] values.
# Causal masking aligns the LAST query with the LAST key, so m <= n and the same
# code path serves prefill (m == n) and decode (m == 1).
q, k, v = (torch.randn(2, 4, 256, 64) for _ in range(3))

# 1. The one-liner. `k=32` is top-k's budget: the tensors are positional, so the
#    short name is free for the method's own configuration.
y = ab.attend("topk", q, k, v, causal=True, k=32)
print("attend      ", tuple(y.shape))

# 2. The object, when you want the weights, the compressed values or the diagnostics.
attn = ab.build("topk", k=32)
out = attn(q, k, v, causal=True, return_weights=True)
print("build       ", out)
print("extras      ", sorted(out.extras))

# 3. The comparison, scored against dense softmax.
rows = ab.compare(["softmax", "flash", "topk", "window", "performer"], q, k, v,
                  causal=True,
                  configs={"topk": {"k": 32}, "window": {"w": 32}, "performer": {"r": 128}})
print(f"\n{'method':<12}{'output err':>12}{'distributional':>16}{'value':>10}")
for r in rows:
    print(f"{r['name']:<12}{r['output_error']:>12.2e}"
          f"{r.get('distributional_error', float('nan')):>16.2e}"
          f"{r.get('value_error', float('nan')):>10.2e}")

docs.title: Invariant W: every method is a measure times a value field
docs.text:
y == weights @ (v_hat if v_hat is not None else value) holds for every registered method -- that is the claim the library is built on, and here it is, checked over the whole bank in float64.

A method that genuinely cannot express its measure on the original n positions sets expresses_weights = False and returns weights=None; it is then excluded from the error decomposition by declaration, which is visible in the output below.

docs.title: The script
docs.text:
examples/02_the_invariant.py
"""
Invariant W: every method is a measure times a value field
==========================================================

``y == weights @ (v_hat if v_hat is not None else value)`` holds for every registered
method -- that is the claim the library is built on, and here it is, checked over the
whole bank in float64.

A method that genuinely cannot express its measure on the original ``n`` positions sets
``expresses_weights = False`` and returns ``weights=None``; it is then excluded from the
error decomposition *by declaration*, which is visible in the output below.
"""
import torch

import attnbank as ab

torch.manual_seed(0)
q, k, v = (torch.randn(1, 2, 24, 16, dtype=torch.float64) for _ in range(3))

print(f"{'method':<18}{'weights':>9}{'v_hat':>8}{'max |y - W v_hat|':>20}")
for name in ab.available():
    out = ab.build(name)(q, k, v, return_weights=True)
    dev = ab.check_invariant(out, v)             # raises if the invariant is violated
    print(f"{name:<18}"
          f"{'yes' if out.weights is not None else '-':>9}"
          f"{'yes' if out.v_hat is not None else '-':>8}"
          f"{dev:>20.2e}")

print("\nnot a single failure -- otherwise check_invariant would have raised.")
print("The same property is asserted in CI for every method, in float32 and float64:")
print("  pytest tests/test_conformance.py -k invariant")

docs.title: Splitting output error into its two causes
docs.text:
An approximation can be wrong in two ways: it attends to the wrong places, or it aggregates the wrong values. metrics.error_decomposition separates them exactly: 

y - y_hat = (pi - pi_hat) v  +  pi_hat (v - v_hat)
            \_____________/    \________________/
            distributional          value

Quantising the KV cache moves error into the value term; restricting the support moves it into the distributional term. Reading one number instead of two hides which.

docs.title: The script
docs.text:
examples/03_error_decomposition.py
"""
Splitting output error into its two causes
==========================================

An approximation can be wrong in two ways: it attends to the wrong places, or it
aggregates the wrong values. ``metrics.error_decomposition`` separates them exactly::

    y - y_hat = (pi - pi_hat) v  +  pi_hat (v - v_hat)
                \\_____________/    \\________________/
                distributional          value

Quantising the KV cache moves error into the *value* term; restricting the support moves
it into the *distributional* term. Reading one number instead of two hides which.
"""
import torch

from attnbank import build, metrics

torch.manual_seed(0)
q, k, v = (torch.randn(1, 4, 128, 64) for _ in range(3))

ref = build("softmax")(q, k, v, causal=True, return_weights=True)

print(f"{'method':<26}{'total':>10}{'distributional':>16}{'value':>10}")
for name, cfg in [("topk", {"k": 16}),
                  ("window", {"w": 16}),
                  ("quantkv", {"bits_k": 16, "bits_v": 2}),
                  ("quantkv", {"bits_k": 2, "bits_v": 16}),
                  ("mla", {"r": 16})]:
    out = build(name, **cfg)(q, k, v, causal=True, return_weights=True)
    d = metrics.error_decomposition(ref.weights, out.weights, v, out.v_hat)
    label = name + " " + ",".join(f"{key}={val}" for key, val in cfg.items())
    print(f"{label:<26}{d['total'].median():>10.3e}"
          f"{d['distributional'].median():>16.3e}{d['value'].median():>10.3e}")

print("""
Read the columns, not the totals. Restriction is purely distributional: it keeps the
values exactly and only moves mass. Quantising values is purely value error.
Quantising keys produces distributional error instead -- the same total can come from
two completely different mechanisms, and only the split tells you which.

Which of the two hurts more is a property of the activations, not of the method; on
real GPT-2 / Qwen2.5 activations it is the keys (study S4, prop:compress-sensitivity).
On the Gaussian inputs above the two are comparable, which is exactly why the paper
runs that study on captured activations rather than on torch.randn.""")

docs.title: Top-k is not output-optimal
docs.text:
Selecting the k largest attention weights minimises the omitted mass eps_q = pi_q(S^c). It does not minimise ||y - y_hat||, because the bound is eps_q * osc(v) and a light token carrying an extreme value can matter more than a heavy token sitting near the mean.

value_topk is the output-aware oracle: same budget, chosen to minimise output error instead. The gap between the two lines below is the cost of selecting on scores alone.

docs.title: The script
docs.text:
examples/04_topk_is_not_output_optimal.py
"""
Top-k is not output-optimal
===========================

Selecting the ``k`` largest attention weights minimises the *omitted mass*
``eps_q = pi_q(S^c)``. It does not minimise ``||y - y_hat||``, because the bound is
``eps_q * osc(v)`` and a light token carrying an extreme value can matter more than a
heavy token sitting near the mean.

``value_topk`` is the output-aware oracle: same budget, chosen to minimise output error
instead. The gap between the two lines below is the cost of selecting on scores alone.
"""
import torch

import attnbank as ab

torch.manual_seed(0)
q, k, v = (torch.randn(1, 2, 64, 32) for _ in range(3))

print(f"{'budget k':>9}{'topk':>12}{'value_topk':>12}{'ratio':>8}")
for budget in (2, 4, 8, 16):
    rows = {r["name"]: r for r in
            ab.compare(["topk", "value_topk"], q, k, v, causal=True,
                       configs={"topk": {"k": budget},
                                "value_topk": {"k": budget, "chunk": 16}})}
    a, b = rows["topk"]["output_error"], rows["value_topk"]["output_error"]
    print(f"{budget:>9}{a:>12.3e}{b:>12.3e}{a / max(b, 1e-30):>8.2f}x")

print("\nSame budget, same inputs, strictly smaller error -- so the selection rule, not")
print("the budget, is what is being measured. Both are oracles: they see the true")
print("scores. A deployable selector (blocktopk, lsh_sample, evict_h2o) can only do")
print("worse than `topk`, which is why `topk` is the right upper bound to quote.")

docs.title: Random features: the error that shrinks, and the error that does not
docs.text:
FAVOR+ (performer) estimates exp(<q, k>) with r positive random features. More features, less error -- and the conformance suite checks that this is monotone, because for a Monte-Carlo method "reduces to softmax at some finite setting" is not available as a correctness anchor.

linear_elu uses a fixed feature map instead. It does not converge to softmax at any r, and it is not trying to: it declares objective = modify. Watch the two columns separate.

docs.title: The script
docs.text:
examples/05_random_features_converge.py
"""
Random features: the error that shrinks, and the error that does not
====================================================================

FAVOR+ (``performer``) estimates ``exp(<q, k>)`` with ``r`` positive random features.
More features, less error -- and the conformance suite checks that this is monotone,
because for a Monte-Carlo method "reduces to softmax at some finite setting" is not
available as a correctness anchor.

``linear_elu`` uses a *fixed* feature map instead. It does not converge to softmax at
any ``r``, and it is not trying to: it declares ``objective = modify``. Watch the two
columns separate.
"""
import torch

import attnbank as ab

torch.manual_seed(0)
q, k, v = (0.5 * torch.randn(1, 2, 64, 32, dtype=torch.float64) for _ in range(3))
ref = ab.build("softmax")(q, k, v).y

fixed = (ab.build("linear_elu")(q, k, v).y - ref).norm(dim=-1).mean()

print(f"{'r':>6}{'performer (approximate)':>26}{'linear_elu (modify)':>22}")
for r in (8, 32, 128, 512, 2048):
    err = torch.stack([(ab.build("performer", r=r, seed=s)(q, k, v).y - ref).norm(dim=-1).mean()
                       for s in range(4)]).mean()
    print(f"{r:>6}{err:>26.4f}{fixed:>22.4f}")

print("\nThe left column is an approximation converging; the right one is a different")
print("operator, measured against a target it never claimed. ab.describe('linear_elu')")
print("says so in the 'objective' field, and the suite exempts it from the anchor.")

docs.title: Attention-matrix error is not output error
docs.text:
Most of the literature reports ||P - P_hat||_F. The quantity a model actually feels is ||(P - P_hat) V||. They are not the same ranking: the Frobenius norm charges a method for mass it moved between two tokens with nearly identical values, which costs the output nothing.

Rank the same methods by both and watch the order change.

docs.title: The script
docs.text:
examples/06_matrix_error_is_not_output_error.py
"""
Attention-matrix error is not output error
==========================================

Most of the literature reports ``||P - P_hat||_F``. The quantity a model actually feels
is ``||(P - P_hat) V||``. They are not the same ranking: the Frobenius norm charges a
method for mass it moved between two tokens with nearly identical values, which costs
the output nothing.

Rank the same methods by both and watch the order change.
"""
import torch

import attnbank as ab

torch.manual_seed(0)
q, k, v = (torch.randn(1, 4, 128, 64) for _ in range(3))

rows = ab.compare(["topk", "window", "sink_window", "blocktopk", "performer", "nystrom"],
                  q, k, v,
                  configs={"topk": {"k": 16}, "window": {"w": 16},
                           "sink_window": {"sinks": 4, "w": 12},
                           "blocktopk": {"block": 8, "n_blocks": 2},
                           "performer": {"r": 64}, "nystrom": {"r": 16}})

by_fro = [r["name"] for r in sorted(rows, key=lambda r: r["matrix_fro"])]
by_out = [r["name"] for r in sorted(rows, key=lambda r: r["output_error"])]

print(f"{'method':<14}{'||P-P_hat||_F':>15}{'||(P-P_hat)V||':>16}{'output err':>12}")
for r in sorted(rows, key=lambda r: r["output_error"]):
    print(f"{r['name']:<14}{r['matrix_fro']:>15.4f}{r['matrix_AV_fro']:>16.4f}"
          f"{r['output_error']:>12.4f}")

print(f"\nranked by Frobenius: {' < '.join(by_fro)}")
print(f"ranked by output:    {' < '.join(by_out)}")
print("\nSpearman between the two rankings is what study S1 reports across configurations;")
print("`metrics.spearman` computes it, and `matrix_AV_fro` is the matrix-level norm that")
print("does control the output.")

docs.title: Finding your way around the bank
docs.text: Thirty-odd methods is too many to remember and too few to need a search engine. Four calls cover it: categories for the taxonomy, list_methods for the table, available for the names, describe for one method in full.

docs.title: The script
docs.text:
examples/07_browse_the_bank.py
"""
Finding your way around the bank
================================

Thirty-odd methods is too many to remember and too few to need a search engine. Four
calls cover it: ``categories`` for the taxonomy, ``list_methods`` for the table,
``available`` for the names, ``describe`` for one method in full.
"""
import attnbank as ab

print("THE TAXONOMY -- what each category changes in y(q) = int v dpi_q\n")
for name, what in ab.categories().items():
    print(f"  {name:<13}{what}")

print("\n\nTHE TABLE -- grouped, with the declaration columns that drive the test suite")
print(ab.list_methods("factorize"))

print("\n\nFILTERS -- every question about the bank is one call")
print("  causal + row-stochastic:", ab.list_methods(causal=True).filter(
    row_stochastic=True).names)
print("  a different operator:   ", ab.available(objective="modify"))
print("  cannot express weights: ", [n for n in ab.available()
                                     if not ab.get_class(n).expresses_weights])

print("\n\nONE METHOD IN FULL\n")
print(ab.describe("nystrom"))

print("\n\nAND THE CONTRACT, ON DEMAND\n")
print(ab.check_conformance("nystrom", r=8))

docs.title: What a method actually saves
docs.text:
Every method declares an analytic cost model: flops, state_bytes (the resident KV cache) and bytes_moved. Decoding is bandwidth-bound, so bytes_moved -- not flops -- is the number that predicts latency, and state_bytes is the number that decides whether the context fits at all.

The conformance suite asserts that any method claiming to save capacity really does have state_bytes <= softmax at a long context. Here is that table.

docs.title: The script
docs.text:
examples/08_cost_and_capacity.py
"""
What a method actually saves
============================

Every method declares an analytic cost model: ``flops``, ``state_bytes`` (the resident
KV cache) and ``bytes_moved``. Decoding is bandwidth-bound, so ``bytes_moved`` -- not
``flops`` -- is the number that predicts latency, and ``state_bytes`` is the number
that decides whether the context fits at all.

The conformance suite asserts that any method claiming to save capacity really does
have ``state_bytes <= softmax`` at a long context. Here is that table.
"""
import attnbank as ab

M, N, D, DV = 1, 4096, 128, 128          # one decode step against a 4k context
dense = ab.build("softmax").cost(M, N, D, DV)

print(f"decode step, n = {N}, d = dv = {D}, fp16\n")
print(f"{'method':<18}{'GFLOPs':>10}{'state MB':>11}{'vs dense':>10}{'bytes moved MB':>16}")
rows = [(name, ab.build(name).cost(M, N, D, DV)) for name in ab.available()]
for name, c in sorted(rows, key=lambda r: r[1]["state_bytes"]):
    print(f"{name:<18}{c['flops'] / 1e9:>10.4f}{c['state_bytes'] / 2**20:>11.2f}"
          f"{c['state_bytes'] / dense['state_bytes']:>10.2f}"
          f"{c['bytes_moved'] / 2**20:>16.2f}")

print("""
The top of the table is the set of methods whose resident state does not grow with n:
windows and evictions keep a fixed number of tokens, recurrences keep a fixed-size
matrix, factorisations keep r latents. That is the whole content of 'finite state' --
and prop:memory-rank is the price: recall is bounded by what the state can hold
(study S6).

Note how little `flops` tells you. `blocktopk` has the fewest and one of the largest
caches; `softmax` and `flash` have identical cost models, because flash changes the
evaluation and not the operator. At decode it is `bytes_moved` that sets the clock
(eq:exact-decode-intensity, study S8).""")

docs.title: Adding a method: declare, implement, conform
docs.text:
Three steps. Subclass attnbank.AttentionMethod, declare what the method is, implement _forward. The declaration is not documentation -- the conformance suite reads it and tests the method against it, so a wrong declaration is a failing build.

The method below keeps the k largest weights and every position in the first s sinks, a sort of hand-rolled StreamingLLM. It is registered under a name that will not collide with the shipped bank.

docs.title: The script
docs.text:
examples/09_add_your_own_method.py
"""
Adding a method: declare, implement, conform
============================================

Three steps. Subclass :class:`attnbank.AttentionMethod`, declare what the method *is*,
implement ``_forward``. The declaration is not documentation -- the conformance suite
reads it and tests the method against it, so a wrong declaration is a failing build.

The method below keeps the ``k`` largest weights *and* every position in the first
``s`` sinks, a sort of hand-rolled StreamingLLM. It is registered under a name that
will not collide with the shipped bank.
"""
import torch

import attnbank as ab


@ab.register
class SinkTopK(ab.AttentionMethod):
    """Top-k on the true scores, with the first ``sinks`` positions always retained."""

    name = "example_sink_topk"
    category = ab.Category.RESTRICT      # it changes the support of pi_q
    objective = ab.Objective.APPROXIMATE  # it targets dense softmax
    supports_causal = True
    expresses_weights = True              # it can name pi_hat on the original n
    row_stochastic = True                 # ... and those weights are a distribution
    trainable = False
    references = ("xiao2024efficient",)
    paper_section = "sec:sparse"

    def __init__(self, k: int | None = 8, sinks: int = 2, **kw):
        super().__init__(k=k, sinks=sinks, **kw)
        self.k, self.sinks = k, sinks

    def _forward(self, q, k, v, causal, return_weights):
        pi = ab.masked_softmax(ab.scores(q, k, self._scale(q.shape[-1]), causal))
        n = k.shape[-2]
        keep = torch.zeros_like(pi, dtype=torch.bool)
        keep[..., :min(self.sinks, n)] = True
        if self.k is not None:
            idx = pi.topk(min(self.k, n), dim=-1).indices
            keep.scatter_(-1, idx, True)
        else:
            keep |= pi > 0
        pi_hat = ab.renormalize(pi * keep)
        return ab.AttentionOutput(y=pi_hat @ v,
                                  weights=pi_hat if return_weights else None,
                                  extras={"omitted_mass": (pi * ~keep).sum(-1)})

    def cost(self, m, n, d, dv, bytes_per_el=2):
        kk = (self.k or n) + self.sinks
        return {"flops": 2 * m * n * d + 2 * m * kk * dv,
                "state_bytes": n * (d + dv) * bytes_per_el,
                "bytes_moved": (m * d + n * d + m * kk * dv) * bytes_per_el}

    @classmethod
    def limit_config(cls):
        # k = None keeps every visible key, so the method reduces to dense softmax.
        return {"k": None}


print(ab.describe("example_sink_topk"))
print()
print(ab.check_conformance("example_sink_topk"))
print()
print("It is now a first-class member of the bank:")
print("  ", ab.available("restrict"))
print("  ", ab.compare(["topk", "example_sink_topk"],
                       *(torch.randn(1, 2, 32, 16) for _ in range(3)), causal=True,
                       configs={"topk": {"k": 4}, "example_sink_topk": {"k": 4}})[1])
print("\nThe full eleven-point suite runs it automatically, because it is parametrized")
print("over the registry: `pytest tests/test_conformance.py`.")

docs.title: Backends: the operator stays, the execution path changes
docs.text:
A method is two things: an operator (the mathematics, one readable file) and an execution path. The operator never changes with the backend -- and that is a tested claim, not a slogan.

Most of the bank declares reference only, and that is the correct answer rather than an omission: an operator that is not a dense softmax over a mask, or whose extras need the full score matrix anyway, has no kernel to dispatch to.

docs.title: The script
docs.text:
examples/10_backends.py
"""
Backends: the operator stays, the execution path changes
========================================================

A method is two things: an *operator* (the mathematics, one readable file) and an
*execution path*. The operator never changes with the backend -- and that is a tested
claim, not a slogan.

Most of the bank declares ``reference`` only, and that is the correct answer rather
than an omission: an operator that is not a dense softmax over a mask, or whose
``extras`` need the full score matrix anyway, has no kernel to dispatch to.
"""
import warnings

import torch

import attnbank as ab

print("WHAT THIS MACHINE CAN RUN\n")
print(ab.backends())

print("\n\nWHO DECLARES WHAT\n")
matrix = ab.backend_matrix()
fast = {n: b for n, b in matrix.items() if len(b) > 1}
for name, declared in fast.items():
    print(f"  {name:<12}{', '.join(declared)}")
only = [n for n, b in matrix.items() if len(b) == 1]
print(f"\n  reference only ({len(only)}): {', '.join(only)}")
print("\n  Not a gap in the library -- a fact about the operators. `nmf_oracle` is an")
print("  oracle factorisation, `merge_kv` is a clustering step, `topk` needs the full")
print("  score matrix for the omitted mass it reports. None of them is a kernel call.")

print("\n\nEQUALITY, ON DEMAND\n")
torch.manual_seed(0)
q, k, v = (torch.randn(2, 4, 64, 32, dtype=torch.float64) for _ in range(3))
for name in fast:
    ref = ab.build(name, backend="reference")(q, k, v, causal=True).y
    for backend in matrix[name][1:]:
        if not ab.is_backend_available(backend):
            info = ab.backend_info(backend)
            print(f"  {name:<10}{backend:<12}skipped: {info.reason}")
            continue
        got = ab.build(name, backend=backend)(q, k, v, causal=True).y
        print(f"  {name:<10}{backend:<12}max |y - y_reference| = "
              f"{float((got - ref).abs().max()):.2e}")

print("\n\nNOTHING IS SILENT\n")
try:
    ab.build("topk", backend="sdpa")
except ab.BackendNotSupportedError as e:
    print("  explicit request for an undeclared backend ->", type(e).__name__)
    print("   ", str(e)[:150], "...")

with warnings.catch_warnings(record=True) as caught:
    warnings.simplefilter("always")
    ab.build("softmax", backend="sdpa")(q, k, v, return_weights=True)
print("\n  asking a fused kernel for the attention weights ->",
      caught[0].category.__name__ if caught else "no warning")
print("   ", str(caught[0].message)[:150] if caught else "")

print("\n  The default is 'reference', and the eight studies pin it explicitly, so no")
print("  published number can move because a faster path appeared:",
      repr(ab.get_default_backend()))

docs.title: Browse the bank
docs.text:
32 methods, every one of them introspectable. The table below is the registry — ab.list_methods() prints the same rows in a terminal, and ab.method_table() returns them as JSON. Each row leads with the name the method is known by and carries its registry key underneath, because the key is what you pass to ab.build(...) and what the method's own page is filed under.

Searching matches both of those, plus the summary, the category, the objective, the backends, the config keys, the BibTeX keys, and words you would plausibly type instead of a flag — causal, trainable, oracle, signed. The filters are plain client-side JavaScript over the table that is already on the page: with scripting off you get all 32 rows, sorted by category, which is the whole content.

Three of these are oracles

value_topk, nmf_oracle and svd_oracle are upper bounds on what a mechanism can achieve, not practical methods — you cannot show that top-\(k\) selection is suboptimal without computing what the optimal selection would have been. They are tagged oracle in the table and carry a banner on their own pages.

docs.title: Quest-style page / block selection
docs.text:
blocktopk · ab.build("blocktopk")

Quest-style page / block selection: restriction at block granularity.

category restrict — one of the seven objects in \(y(q)=\int v\,\mathrm{d}\pi_q\) a method can change objective approximate — targets fidelity to dense softmax; judged by output error class attnbank.BlockTopKAttention, attnbank/methods/restrict/blocktopk.py monograph sec:sparse

docs.title: What it changes
docs.text:
Changes the support of \(\pi_q\), which shrinks to \(S_q \subseteq \{1,\dots,n\}\) and is renormalised on it. The values \(v\) are untouched, so the whole error is distributional.

It pursues approximation: it is trying to be dense softmax, so it is fair to judge it by output error, and it must supply a correctness anchor saying where it becomes exact.

docs.title: In the paper's notation
docs.text:
sec:sparse-query ("Blocks and pages") and prop:sparse-certificate. Keys are partitioned into contiguous pages of block positions. A page is ranked by an upper bound on the scores it can contain,

tau(B) = beta * sum_c max( q_c * kmin_{B,c},  q_c * kmax_{B,c} ),

from the elementwise minima and maxima of the keys in the page (Tang et al., 2024). The top n_blocks pages are fetched and attended exactly; everything else is omitted, so the error is again eps_q (m_{S^c} - m_S).

The point of having it alongside topk is granularity: a page-level selector can only ever omit or retain whole pages, so its realized eps_q exceeds the top-k minimum by a selection error. score="max" and score="mean" are provided to separate the cost of the bound from the cost of the granularity: the paper notes that an upper bound never misses a page containing a heavy key but may waste budget, whereas a pooled representative can average a heavy key away.

Causality. Page statistics are computed over whole pages, so only complete past pages may be ranked. The page containing the query's own position is always selected (as in Quest, where the current page is resident anyway) and later pages are excluded. This makes the support depend on nothing after the query.

docs.title: What it declares
docs.text:
Each row is a commitment the conformance suite tests, not a description.

attribute declared what that commits it to supports_causal yes causal=True masks so query \(i\) sees keys \(0 \dots i + (n-m)\). expresses_weights yes it can name \(\widehat\pi_q\) on the original \(n\) positions, so it enters the error decomposition. row_stochastic yes those weights are \(\ge 0\) and sum to one: \(\widehat\pi_q\) is a probability measure. head_independent yes each head is computed from its own \(K, V\). trainable no no learned parameters — what you build is what the paper describes.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
parameter default block 4 n_blocks 2 score 'bound'

score: 'bound' (Quest), 'max' (exact page maximum) or 'mean'.

ab.describe("blocktopk")     # the same keys, with everything else it declares

docs.title: Correctness anchor
docs.text:
Exact limit. Built with n_blocks=None this method provably is dense softmax, and tests/test_conformance.py asserts it — output and weights, float32 and float64.

>>> ab.describe("blocktopk").limit_config
{'n_blocks': None}

docs.title: Backends
docs.text:
backend what it is reference plain PyTorch; the correctness anchor and the default

reference only, and that is the correct answer. It reports the omitted mass eps (and the \(\chi^2\) divergence of the renormalisation) in extras, which needs the full score matrix. A kernel that avoids materialising that matrix is a kernel that cannot produce them.

Declaring a backend is a claim that it equals the reference, checked by tests/test_conformance.py::test_backend_equivalence; declaring sdpa here would be pretending. See Backends.

Diagnostics returned in extras: chi2, eps, k_realized, n_pages, page_scores, page_size, pages_selected, support.

docs.title: Cost model
docs.text:
Analytic, per (batch, head), declared by the method itself:

def cost(self, m, n, d, dv, bytes_per_el=2):
    nb = (n + self.block - 1) // self.block
    kept = min(self.n_blocks or nb, nb) * self.block
    return {"flops": 2 * m * nb * d + 2 * m * kept * (d + dv),
            "state_bytes": n * (d + dv) * bytes_per_el + 2 * nb * d * bytes_per_el,

docs.title: Clustered attention
docs.text:
clustered · ab.build("clustered")

Clustered attention: route queries through r query centroids.

category factorize — one of the seven objects in \(y(q)=\int v\,\mathrm{d}\pi_q\) a method can change objective approximate — targets fidelity to dense softmax; judged by output error class attnbank.ClusteredAttention, attnbank/methods/factorize/clustered.py monograph sec:factor

docs.title: What it changes
docs.text:
Changes the shape of \(\pi_q\): it is routed through \(r\) latents, \(\pi_q = a(q,\cdot)\,b(\cdot,x)\), which caps the rank of the attention matrix at \(r\).

It pursues approximation: it is trying to be dense softmax, so it is fair to judge it by output error, and it must supply a correctness anchor saying where it becomes exact.

docs.title: In the paper's notation
docs.text:
sec:factor-methods. The queries are clustered; one attention row is computed per centroid and shared by every query in the cluster:

pi_hat_{q_i} = softmax_x( beta <c_{g(i)}, k_x> ).

In the language of def:factor-stochastic this is P_hat = A B with A the (0/1) cluster-assignment matrix — row-stochastic — and B the r centroid rows, also row-stochastic: a latent stochastic factorization whose latent space is a partition of the queries rather than of the context. It therefore inherits all of prop:factor-closure.

Unlike latent_stochastic it is an approximation with a resource parameter: r = None gives every query its own cluster and reproduces softmax exactly, which is the correctness anchor. Its error is controlled by how far a query sits from its centroid, via prop:error-score with delta = beta ||q - c|| max_j ||k_j||.

Not causal: queries in one cluster have different visibility, so a shared row would leak. Clustering is Lloyd's algorithm with a seeded initialization.

attribute declared what that commits it to supports_causal no causal=True raises CausalNotSupportedError — a statement about the operator, not a missing feature. expresses_weights yes it can name \(\widehat\pi_q\) on the original \(n\) positions, so it enters the error decomposition. row_stochastic yes those weights are \(\ge 0\) and sum to one: \(\widehat\pi_q\) is a probability measure. head_independent yes each head is computed from its own \(K, V\). trainable no no learned parameters — what you build is what the paper describes.

docs.title: cosFormer
docs.text:
cosformer · ab.build("cosformer")

CosFormer: ReLU features with a cosine re-weighting.

category interaction — one of the seven objects in \(y(q)=\int v\,\mathrm{d}\pi_q\) a method can change objective modify — defines a different operator; fidelity to softmax is not the goal class attnbank.CosFormerAttention, attnbank/methods/interaction/cosformer.py monograph sec:kernel

docs.title: What it changes
docs.text:
Changes the interaction \(g(q,x)\), replaced by a surrogate \(\widehat g\). \(\pi_q = \widehat g(q,\cdot)\mu / \widehat Z(q)\) is then a different measure on the same \(n\) positions.

It pursues modification: it defines a different operator. Asking how closely it approximates softmax is asking the wrong question — it is not trying to.

docs.title: In the paper's notation
docs.text:
sec:kernel-det. Qin et al. (2022) use

g_hat(q_i, k_j) = relu(q_i)^T relu(k_j) * cos(pi (i - j) / (2 M)),   M >= n,

separable with 2r features via cos(a - a') = cos a cos a' + sin a sin a'. The cosine factor injects a locality prior: the re-weighting decays monotonically with |i - j| and stays nonnegative because |i - j| <= n - 1 < M keeps the argument inside [-pi/2, pi/2], so pi_hat_q remains a probability measure.

Like linear_elu this is a fixed feature map with no resource parameter: an operator modification (tab:kernel-methods: "cosFormer ... no"), and rem:kernel-homogeneous applies exactly, since relu is positively homogeneous — scaling the query cannot change pi_hat_q at all.

Positions follow the library's end-alignment convention: query i sits at absolute context position i + (n - m).

docs.title: Decayed linear recurrence
docs.text:
decay_rnn · ab.build("decay_rnn")

Decayed linear recurrence: H_t = gamma H_{t-1} + psi(k_t) v_t^T.

category recurrent — one of the seven objects in \(y(q)=\int v\,\mathrm{d}\pi_q\) a method can change objective modify — defines a different operator; fidelity to softmax is not the goal class attnbank.DecayRNNAttention, attnbank/methods/recurrent/decay_rnn.py monograph sec:memory-state

docs.title: What it changes
docs.text:
Changes the operator. \(y\) is produced by a finite-state recurrence over positions rather than by an integral against a measure — though it is still linear in \(v\), which is why the weights can be recovered at all.

It pursues modification: it defines a different operator. Asking how closely it approximates softmax is asking the wrong question — it is not trying to.

docs.title: In the paper's notation
docs.text:
sec:memory-state, tab:memory-recurrences (rows "Retention", "GLA / Mamba-2"). A_t = gamma Id with a fixed gamma < 1 is retention (RetNet); a data-dependent scalar or diagonal gate gives Mamba-2, GLA, HGRN2, RWKV-5/6 and the mLSTM. The weights on the original positions are

w_{tj} = gamma^{(t - j)} <phi(q_t), psi(k_j)>,    j <= t,

an exponential recency prior multiplying a rank-r content term.

Decay restores boundedness without restoring normalization: the effective mass sum_i prod_{u>i} gamma_u is bounded by 1/(1 - gamma) rather than growing with n, so the output cannot blow up with context length, but it is still not an expectation under a probability measure (set normalize=True to recover one). This is the distinction sec:memory-state draws between "restoring boundedness" and "restoring the contract".

State size is r x d_v regardless of gamma, so sweeping gamma at fixed state separates recency from capacity — which is what study S6 needs.

docs.title: DeltaNet
docs.text:
delta_rnn · ab.build("delta_rnn")

DeltaNet: the delta-rule update on a fast-weight memory.

category recurrent — one of the seven objects in \(y(q)=\int v\,\mathrm{d}\pi_q\) a method can change objective modify — defines a different operator; fidelity to softmax is not the goal class attnbank.DeltaRNNAttention, attnbank/methods/recurrent/delta_rnn.py monograph sec:memory-state

docs.title: What it changes
docs.text:
Changes the operator. \(y\) is produced by a finite-state recurrence over positions rather than by an integral against a measure — though it is still linear in \(v\), which is why the weights can be recovered at all.

It pursues modification: it defines a different operator. Asking how closely it approximates softmax is asking the wrong question — it is not trying to.

docs.title: In the paper's notation
docs.text:
sec:memory-state, eq:memory-delta, tab:memory-recurrences (row "DeltaNet"). The transition is a rank-one correction rather than a decay:

H_t = (I - beta_t psi_t psi_t^T) H_{t-1} + beta_t psi_t v_t^T,    psi_t = psi(k_t),
y_hat_t = H_t^T phi(q_t),

which is exactly one gradient step of size beta_t on the per-token regression loss L_t(H) = 1/2 ||H^T psi_t - v_t||^2 (Widrow–Hoff). Plain linear attention is a gradient step on the linear loss -<H^T psi_t, v_t>, which never saturates and so never corrects interference between non-orthogonal keys; the delta rule does. That is the whole capacity argument: at a fixed state of r x d_v, the delta rule stores more distinguishable associations than the additive recurrence, which is what study S6 measures.

The regression view also identifies the operator. Softmax attention is a Nadaraya–Watson estimator that never leaves the convex hull of the stored values; the delta rule fits a global parametric regression of v on psi(k) online and returns arbitrary linear combinations. It is a new operator and is judged by downstream quality, not by fidelity to y(q).

Weights. H_t is linear in V, so H_t = M_t V for an r x n coefficient matrix obeying the same recurrence driven by the basis vectors, M_t = (I - beta psi_t psi_t^T) M_{t-1} + beta psi_t e_t^T. Running it gives the exact weights w_{tj} = <phi(q_t), M_t[:, j]> at a cost of O(n^2 r), which is the price of exposing pi_hat on the original positions. psi is l2-normalized, as in DeltaNet, so that I - beta psi psi^T is a contraction for beta in (0, 2).

Note on notation: DESIGN.md writes the update as H_{t-1}(I - beta phi phi^T), which is the same map with H transposed (d_v x r). This file follows the paper's eq:memory-delta with H in R^{r x d_v}.

docs.title: H2O
docs.text:
evict_h2o · ab.build("evict_h2o")

H2O: accumulated-attention heavy-hitter eviction plus a recent window.

category compress — one of the seven objects in \(y(q)=\int v\,\mathrm{d}\pi_q\) a method can change objective approximate — targets fidelity to dense softmax; judged by output error class attnbank.H2OAttention, attnbank/methods/compress/evict_h2o.py monograph sec:compress

docs.title: What it changes
docs.text:
Changes the stored context \((\mu, k, v)\) itself. This is the one category that routinely perturbs the integrand, so \(\widehat v \neq v\) and the error has a value term.

It pursues approximation: it is trying to be dense softmax, so it is fair to judge it by output error, and it must supply a correctness anchor saying where it becomes exact.

docs.title: In the paper's notation
docs.text:
sec:compress-evict, prop:compress-noeviction. Eviction is a restriction whose set is chosen before the queries that will use it exist, and the sets are nested: S_{t+1} subset S_t union {t+1}. A deleted token is gone for every future query, so prop:compress-noeviction says no query-oblivious rule has a uniform guarantee — for any retained S and any evicted j, the query q = tau k_j drives eps_q -> 1 while y_hat stays in conv{v_i : i in S}.

H2O estimates the future-query distribution nu by the empirical distribution of past queries: token j is scored by sum_{t' <= t} pi_{q_{t'}}(j), and the lowest-scoring non-recent token is dropped whenever the cache exceeds its budget. This file runs that process literally, one query at a time, which is why it is causal: the state at step t depends on keys and queries up to t only.

In non-causal mode the whole context is admitted at the first step and the same accumulate-and-evict loop runs over the queries in order; the semantics are then "a streaming cache served by a fixed context".

Exact limit: budget = None (no eviction).

docs.title: SnapKV
docs.text:
evict_snapkv · ab.build("evict_snapkv")

SnapKV: prompt-token scores pooled over an observation window.

category compress — one of the seven objects in \(y(q)=\int v\,\mathrm{d}\pi_q\) a method can change objective approximate — targets fidelity to dense softmax; judged by output error class attnbank.SnapKVAttention, attnbank/methods/compress/evict_snapkv.py monograph sec:compress

docs.title: What it changes
docs.text:
Changes the stored context \((\mu, k, v)\) itself. This is the one category that routinely perturbs the integrand, so \(\widehat v \neq v\) and the error has a value term.

It pursues approximation: it is trying to be dense softmax, so it is fair to judge it by output error, and it must supply a correctness anchor saying where it becomes exact.

docs.title: In the paper's notation
docs.text:
sec:compress-evict ("Estimating importance from past queries"). SnapKV scores prompt tokens with the attention of the last obs prompt queries, applies a 1-D pooling of width pool along the key axis so that whole local neighbourhoods are kept rather than isolated tokens, keeps the top budget - recent of them, and adds the recent window. The compressed cache then serves all subsequent decoding queries.

This works when the question ends the prompt — the observation window is then a good sample of nu in eq:compress-evict-objective — and degrades when it arrives earlier.

Not causal, deliberately. The support is chosen after seeing the whole prompt and is then applied to every query, including earlier ones. That is what SnapKV does in a prefill-then-decode pipeline, and it cannot be expressed as a causally masked single forward pass: query 0's support would depend on query m-1. Declaring supports_causal = False records the fact rather than hiding it behind a mask.

Exact limit: budget = None.

docs.title: FlashAttention
docs.text:
flash · ab.build("flash")

FlashAttention: tiled online softmax (sec:exact, sec:exact-tiling).

category exact — one of the seven objects in \(y(q)=\int v\,\mathrm{d}\pi_q\) a method can change objective accelerate — same operator, exact up to floating point; only the evaluation changes class attnbank.FlashAttention, attnbank/methods/exact/flash.py monograph sec:exact

docs.title: What it changes
docs.text:
Changes nothing in \(y(q)=\int v\,\mathrm{d}\pi_q\). The integrand, the measure and the normaliser are the reference operator's; only the order of arithmetic changes.

It pursues acceleration: the operator is the reference operator, exact up to floating point. The only question worth asking of it is where exactness stops.

docs.title: In the paper's notation
docs.text:
The operator is unchanged. For a block J of key indices the partial state is

sigma_J = (a_J, l_J, u_J),
a_J = max_{j in J} s_j,  l_J = sum_{j in J} e^{s_j - a_J},  u_J = sum_{j in J} e^{s_j - a_J} v_j,

with merge (eq:exact-merge)

(a1,l1,u1) + (a2,l2,u2) = (a, e^{a1-a} l1 + e^{a2-a} l2, e^{a1-a} u1 + e^{a2-a} u2),
a = max(a1, a2),

readout rd(a,l,u) = u/l and identity (-inf, 0, 0). prop:exact-monoid states that (Sigma, +, 0) is a commutative monoid and that the readout of the fold over any partition is y(q). This file folds left-to-right over key blocks in one pass, which is what a FlashAttention kernel does.

The monoid itself lives in attnbank.components.online_softmax, shared with splitk; this file is only the decision to fold it left-to-right in one pass.

docs.title: Grouped-query attention
docs.text:
gqa · ab.build("gqa")

Grouped-query attention: K and V shared across groups of query heads.

category compress — one of the seven objects in \(y(q)=\int v\,\mathrm{d}\pi_q\) a method can change objective modify — defines a different operator; fidelity to softmax is not the goal class attnbank.GQAAttention, attnbank/methods/compress/gqa.py monograph sec:compress

docs.title: What it changes
docs.text:
Changes the stored context \((\mu, k, v)\) itself. This is the one category that routinely perturbs the integrand, so \(\widehat v \neq v\) and the error has a value term.

It pursues modification: it defines a different operator. Asking how closely it approximates softmax is asking the wrong question — it is not trying to.

docs.title: In the paper's notation
docs.text:
sec:compress-arch, sec:exact-roofline. Query heads are partitioned into groups of group_size; the heads of a group share one key–value pair, here obtained by mean-pooling the group's K and V (the conversion recipe of Ainslie et al., 2023). group_size = 1 is multi-head attention, group_size = h is multi-query.

This is an operator modification (tab:comparative: "MQA / GQA / MLA ... mod."), trained as such; measuring it against a multi-head reference answers a conversion question, not an approximation question. Its purpose is the roofline: by eq:exact-decode-intensity the decode arithmetic intensity is (16/b)(h/h_kv), so sharing KV is one of the very few interventions that raises it. cost() divides state_bytes and the KV traffic by group_size accordingly.

Heads are deliberately coupled, so head_independent = False: perturbing head h changes every head in its group and nothing outside it. tests/test_compress.py checks exactly that boundary.

Exact limit: group_size = 1.

docs.title: Latent stochastic factorization
docs.text:
latent_stochastic · ab.build("latent_stochastic")

Latent stochastic factorization: two Markov kernels through r latents.

category factorize — one of the seven objects in \(y(q)=\int v\,\mathrm{d}\pi_q\) a method can change objective modify — defines a different operator; fidelity to softmax is not the goal class attnbank.LatentStochasticAttention, attnbank/methods/factorize/latent_stochastic.py monograph sec:factor

docs.title: What it changes
docs.text:
Changes the shape of \(\pi_q\): it is routed through \(r\) latents, \(\pi_q = a(q,\cdot)\,b(\cdot,x)\), which caps the rank of the attention matrix at \(r\).

It pursues modification: it defines a different operator. Asking how closely it approximates softmax is asking the wrong question — it is not trying to.

docs.title: In the paper's notation
docs.text:
sec:factor-def, def:factor-stochastic, prop:factor-closure. A rank-r latent stochastic factorization is a pair of Markov kernels a: Q -> Z (read) and b: Z -> X (write) with

pi_hat_q(dx) = sum_z a(q, z) b(z, dx),    P_hat = A B,
A in R_{>=0}^{m x r} with A 1 = 1,   B in R_{>=0}^{r x n} with B 1 = 1.

Both kernels are attentions (eq:factor-write, eq:factor-read):

b(z, .) = softmax_x( beta <w_z, k_x> ),     w_z a latent query,
a(q, z) = softmax_z( beta <q, kbar_z> ),    kbar_z = int k_x b(z, dx),

the ABC form in which the latent keys summarize the context rather than being free (Peng et al., 2022). The latent queries w_z are the learned parameters; here they are a seeded Gaussian, so trainable = True records that the method is only meaningful after training.

prop:factor-closure is why this category exists separately from low-rank approximation: a composition of Markov kernels is automatically a probability measure, so normalization, constant preservation and convex-hull confinement all survive — none of which holds for a generic signed rank-r factorization. The output has the two-level form y_hat(q) = sum_z a(q,z) u(z) with u(z) = int v db(z,.), so the context is seen only through r latent values.

This is an operator modification (tab:comparative): there is no r at which it becomes softmax, and nothing it converges to, so both correctness anchors are None by design. It loses fs (full support in the exact sense) and ql.

Not causal: the write kernel pools over the whole context.

docs.title: Linear transformer
docs.text:
linear_elu · ab.build("linear_elu")

Linear transformer: the fixed feature map phi(u) = elu(u) + 1.

category interaction — one of the seven objects in \(y(q)=\int v\,\mathrm{d}\pi_q\) a method can change objective modify — defines a different operator; fidelity to softmax is not the goal class attnbank.LinearELUAttention, attnbank/methods/interaction/linear_elu.py monograph sec:kernel

docs.title: What it changes
docs.text:
Changes the interaction \(g(q,x)\), replaced by a surrogate \(\widehat g\). \(\pi_q = \widehat g(q,\cdot)\mu / \widehat Z(q)\) is then a different measure on the same \(n\) positions.

It pursues modification: it defines a different operator. Asking how closely it approximates softmax is asking the wrong question — it is not trying to.

docs.title: In the paper's notation
docs.text:
sec:kernel-det. Katharopoulos et al. (2020) replace the interaction by

g_hat(q, x) = <phi(q), phi(k_x)>,   phi(u) = elu(u) + 1 > 0,   r = d,

with no resource parameter, so <phi(q), phi(k)> -> exp(beta <q,k>) holds in no sense: this is an operator modification, not an approximation (def:kernel-regimes, tab:kernel-methods row "Linear transformer ... no"). The library records that by objective = modify and by returning None from both correctness anchors: there is no configuration under which it becomes softmax, and nothing it converges to.

Because phi > 0 the induced measure is a genuine probability measure, so this is one of the normalized members of the family; lem:kernel-mixture then says pi_hat_q is a mixture of r = d query-independent context distributions, and prop:kernel-retrieval bounds what it can retrieve. rem:kernel-homogeneous applies approximately: for large positive coordinates phi is linear, so the query norm cannot sharpen pi_hat_q.

The normalized form of eq:kernel-moments is used (divide by phi(q)^T z). Many deployed descendants drop the denominator and normalize the output instead (sec:memory-state); that variant lives in recurrent/linear_rnn.py, where the loss of normalization invariance is the point.

docs.title: Linear attention as a recurrence
docs.text:
linear_rnn · ab.build("linear_rnn")

Linear attention as a recurrence: H_t = H_{t-1} + psi(k_t) v_t^T.

category recurrent — one of the seven objects in \(y(q)=\int v\,\mathrm{d}\pi_q\) a method can change objective modify — defines a different operator; fidelity to softmax is not the goal class attnbank.LinearRNNAttention, attnbank/methods/recurrent/linear_rnn.py monograph sec:memory-state

docs.title: What it changes
docs.text:
Changes the operator. \(y\) is produced by a finite-state recurrence over positions rather than by an integral against a measure — though it is still linear in \(v\), which is why the weights can be recovered at all.

It pursues modification: it defines a different operator. Asking how closely it approximates softmax is asking the wrong question — it is not trying to.

docs.title: In the paper's notation
docs.text:
sec:memory-state, prop:memory-suff, prop:memory-rank. A separable interaction of rank r admits a sufficient statistic of size r x d_v: the prefix moments H_t = sum_{i<=t} psi(k_i) v_i^T (and z_t = sum psi(k_i)) are all a future query needs. prop:memory-rank is the converse: an additive finite-state memory forces the interaction to have finite rank, so recall is bounded by the state.

With the normalizer kept this is linear_elu. The deployed form, and the one here, drops it (readout = H_t^T phi(q_t)) because the denominator can approach zero and produce unbounded gradients. Three properties of eq:attention_expectation go with it (sec:memory-state): normalization invariance under g -> c(q) g, constant preservation (y_hat = c <phi(q), z> now scales with context length), and the convex-hull bound. Set normalize=True to put the denominator back and watch all three return.

The weights on the original positions are w_{tj} = <phi(q_t), psi(k_j)> for j <= t: nonnegative for a positive feature map, but not summing to one. Invariant W still holds exactly, which is why this category is in the library at all.

docs.title: Linformer
docs.text:
linformer · ab.build("linformer")

Linformer: a fixed linear projection of K and V along the sequence axis.

category compress — one of the seven objects in \(y(q)=\int v\,\mathrm{d}\pi_q\) a method can change objective approximate — targets fidelity to dense softmax; judged by output error class attnbank.LinformerAttention, attnbank/methods/compress/linformer.py monograph sec:compress

docs.title: What it changes
docs.text:
Changes the stored context \((\mu, k, v)\) itself. This is the one category that routinely perturbs the integrand, so \(\widehat v \neq v\) and the error has a value term.

It pursues approximation: it is trying to be dense softmax, so it is fair to judge it by output error, and it must supply a correctness anchor saying where it becomes exact.

docs.title: In the paper's notation
docs.text:
sec:compress-lowrank, sec:factor-methods. With E, F in R^{r x n},

P_hat = softmax(beta Q (E K)^T) in R^{m x r},    y_hat = P_hat (F V),

so E K and F V are r learned pseudo-tokens: the method compresses keys and values separately, changes both mu and v, fixes n, and is not causal.

It can be written on the original positions, and that is how the library stores it: y_hat = (P_hat F) V, so weights = P_hat F in R^{m x n} with the original values. Those weights are generally signed and their rows do not sum to one unless F is row-stochastic, which is the paper's point — tab:comparative lists Linformer as losing nm and hl. row_stochastic = False records it, and the row sums are returned in extras so the deviation can be measured.

Note also that the latent keys (EK)_z enter the softmax linearly, and exp(beta <q, sum_x E_zx k_x>) != sum_x E_zx exp(beta <q, k_x>), so the entries of P are not approximated at all; the Johnson–Lindenstrauss argument is an existence statement about the reference operator with random E, F, not an error bound for the trained operator.

Exact limit: r = None sets E = F = I_n, which gives dense softmax.

docs.title: Low-precision attention
docs.text:
lowprec · ab.build("lowprec")

Low-precision attention: simulated FP8 / INT8 logits and values.

category exact — one of the seven objects in \(y(q)=\int v\,\mathrm{d}\pi_q\) a method can change objective approximate — targets fidelity to dense softmax; judged by output error class attnbank.LowPrecisionAttention, attnbank/methods/exact/lowprec.py monograph sec:exact-boundary

docs.title: What it changes
docs.text:
Changes nothing in \(y(q)=\int v\,\mathrm{d}\pi_q\). The integrand, the measure and the normaliser are the reference operator's; only the order of arithmetic changes.

It pursues approximation: it is trying to be dense softmax, so it is fair to judge it by output error, and it must supply a correctness anchor saying where it becomes exact.

docs.title: In the paper's notation
docs.text:
sec:exact-boundary. This is the method that marks where exactness ends. An FP8/INT8 kernel keeps the evaluation order of prop:exact-monoid but stores the operands at a precision u' >> u, so it satisfies the first clause of def:exact-scheme and fails the second. By the criterion of "which object is changed" it belongs with context compression: quantizing q, k replaces g by g_hat (a distributional error) and quantizing v or P replaces v by v_hat (a value-representation error). Its objective is therefore approximate, not accelerate, which is the whole point of putting it in exact/.

Simulation is quantize–dequantize in the kernel, per attention head and per tensor:

Q_b(x) = clamp(round(x / Delta), -2^{b-1}, 2^{b-1} - 1) * Delta,  Delta = max|x| / (2^{b-1} - 1)

for signed INT-b, and round-to-nearest on the FP8 E4M3 / E5M2 grids. Optional incoherent processing (hadamard=True) multiplies q and k by a shared random orthogonal Hadamard matrix before quantizing, which is exact in infinite precision (<Rq, Rk> = <q, k>) and spreads outlier coordinates, as in FlashAttention-3's FP8 path. Optional smoothing (smooth_k=True) subtracts the token mean of k, which shifts every logit of a query by one constant and so leaves pi_q exactly invariant (SageAttention).

The quantizers themselves live in attnbank.components.quantization, shared with quantkv: one implementation, one place where the rounding rule is argued about.

docs.title: What it declares
docs.text:
Each row is a commitment the conformance suite tests, not a description.

attribute declared what that commits it to supports_causal yes causal=True masks so query \(i\) sees keys \(0 \dots i + (n-m)\). expresses_weights yes it can name \(\widehat\pi_q\) on the original \(n\) positions, so it enters the error decomposition. row_stochastic yes those weights are \(\ge 0\) and sum to one: \(\widehat\pi_q\) is a probability measure. head_independent yes each head is computed from its own \(K, V\). trainable no no learned parameters — what you build is what the paper describes.

parameter default bits 8 fmt None bits_p None hadamard_qk False smooth_k False seed 0

bits: INT width for q, k, v (None = no quantization, the exact limit). fmt: 'e4m3' / 'e5m2' to use FP8 instead of INT. bits_p: optional INT width for the attention weights themselves.

docs.title: Hidden-dimension low rank
docs.text:
lowrank_kv · ab.build("lowrank_kv")

Hidden-dimension low rank: truncated SVD of the key and value channel matrices.

category compress — one of the seven objects in \(y(q)=\int v\,\mathrm{d}\pi_q\) a method can change objective approximate — targets fidelity to dense softmax; judged by output error class attnbank.LowRankKVAttention, attnbank/methods/compress/lowrank_kv.py monograph sec:compress

docs.title: What it changes
docs.text:
Changes the stored context \((\mu, k, v)\) itself. This is the one category that routinely perturbs the integrand, so \(\widehat v \neq v\) and the error has a value term.

It pursues approximation: it is trying to be dense softmax, so it is fair to judge it by output error, and it must supply a correctness anchor saying where it becomes exact.

docs.title: In the paper's notation
docs.text:
sec:compress-lowrank. With Pi_r an orthogonal projector of rank r on the channel space,

k_hat_j = Pi_r^K k_j,   v_hat_j = Pi_r^V v_j,

where Pi_r^K and Pi_r^V are the leading right singular subspaces of K and V. The two errors are structurally different, which is the point of the file:

  • Keys. delta_l_j = -beta <(I - Pi_r) q, (I - Pi_r) k_j>, so a subspace chosen from the keys alone fails exactly when the queries load on low-variance key directions — no amount of key energy captured says anything until the query is known.
  • Values. Since pi_hat is unaffected by a value projection, the value error is sum_j pi_j (I - Pi_r) v_j = (I - Pi_r) y(q): the projection residual of the output, not of the approximate output and not of the raw value matrix. So the optimal value subspace is the leading eigenspace of the attention-weighted second moment of the outputs.

Not causal: the SVD pools over all tokens. The factorization is computed in float64 so that the exact limit (rank_k = rank_v = None) is exact to machine precision.

docs.title: LOTFormer-style factored coupling
docs.text:
lowrank_ot · ab.build("lowrank_ot")

LOTFormer-style factored coupling: transport through r pivots.

category coupling — one of the seven objects in \(y(q)=\int v\,\mathrm{d}\pi_q\) a method can change objective modify — defines a different operator; fidelity to softmax is not the goal class attnbank.LowRankOTAttention, attnbank/methods/coupling/lowrank_ot.py monograph sec:ot

docs.title: What it changes
docs.text:
Changes the normalisation. \(Z(q)\) stops being a per-query constant and becomes a global constraint, so the queries are no longer independent of one another.

It pursues modification: it defines a different operator. Asking how closely it approximates softmax is asking the wrong question — it is not trying to.

docs.title: In the paper's notation
docs.text:
sec:ot ("Factorization through a pivot measure"), eq:ot-glued, and eq:factor-pivot. Let rho be a probability measure on r pivots. Given gamma_1 in Pi(nu, rho) and gamma_2 in Pi(rho, mubar), the glued coupling

gamma(dq, dx) = sum_z rho_z gamma_1(dq | z) gamma_2(dx | z)
              = Gamma_1 diag(rho)^{-1} Gamma_2

lies in Pi(nu, mubar), has rank at most r, and has query conditional pi^piv_q = sum_z gamma_1(z | q) gamma_2(. | z). Both halves are solved by Sinkhorn on dot-product costs (queries-to-pivots, pivots-to-keys), so the whole thing costs O((m + n) r) and never forms the m x n matrix.

Two readings of the same object. As a coupling it is doubly stochastic and so balances participation of context positions — no key absorbs the mass of all queries. As a factorization it is exactly def:factor-stochastic: A_{iz} = gamma_1(z|q_i) and B_{zj} = gamma_2(j|z) are both row-stochastic, so prop:factor-closure applies and pi_hat is a probability measure by construction. It is filed under coupling because the column constraint, absent from the row-stochastic factorizations of sec:factor, is the thing it adds.

It is a new operator: a doubly stochastic coupling does not approximate softmax, whose column sums are unconstrained, and it is not claimed to approximate the full plan of prop:ot-conditional either. Hence no exact limit and no convergence sequence — the pivots are learned end to end, so trainable = True.

Not causal, for the reason in prop:ot-causal.

docs.title: LSH importance sampling
docs.text:
lsh_sample · ab.build("lsh_sample")

LSH importance sampling: MagicPIG-style key sampling with unbiased reweighting.

category restrict — one of the seven objects in \(y(q)=\int v\,\mathrm{d}\pi_q\) a method can change objective approximate — targets fidelity to dense softmax; judged by output error class attnbank.LSHSampleAttention, attnbank/methods/restrict/lsh_sample.py monograph sec:sparse

docs.title: What it changes
docs.text:
Changes the support of \(\pi_q\), which shrinks to \(S_q \subseteq \{1,\dots,n\}\) and is renormalised on it. The values \(v\) are untouched, so the whole error is distributional.

It pursues approximation: it is trying to be dense softmax, so it is fair to judge it by output error, and it must supply a correctness anchor saying where it becomes exact.

docs.title: In the paper's notation
docs.text:
sec:sparse-content ("Sampling is not restriction") and prop:error-ratio-est. A key set S is sampled with inclusion probabilities u_j monotone in the attention score, and the output is the self-normalized importance-sampling estimator (eq:sparse-snis)

y_hat(q) = sum_{j in S} (g_j / u_j) v_j  /  sum_{j in S} (g_j / u_j),
pi_hat_j = 1{j in S} (pi_j / u_j) / sum_i 1{i in S} (pi_i / u_i).

Numerator and normalizer are unbiased for N(q) and Z(q); the ratio is only consistent, with O(1/N_s) bias (Owen, 2013). Unlike deterministic restriction this does not systematically reallocate tail mass to the head — it trades the value-dependent bias of prop:sparse-identity for variance, whose size is (1 + chi2(pi || lambda)) / N_s times sup_x ||v(x) - y||^2 (prop:error-ratio-est (b)).

Proposal. MagicPIG derives u_j from SimHash collision probabilities; this reference implementation abstracts that to a tempered proposal lambda_j ∝ exp(alpha * s_j) on the visible keys, with alpha = 0 uniform and alpha = 1 tracking pi exactly, and Poisson (independent Bernoulli) sampling at u_j = min(1, N_s * lambda_j). Sweeping alpha is how chi2(pi || lambda), the quantity the bound is stated in, is varied.

Exact limit. n_samples = None sets u_j = 1 for every visible key, so S is the whole visible context and pi_hat = pi exactly.

Degenerate draw. If a row samples nothing, the single largest-score visible key is inserted so the estimator is defined; the event is counted in extras["empty_draws"].

docs.title: Token merging
docs.text:
merge_kv · ab.build("merge_kv")

Token merging: a pushforward compression of the context measure.

category compress — one of the seven objects in \(y(q)=\int v\,\mathrm{d}\pi_q\) a method can change objective approximate — targets fidelity to dense softmax; judged by output error class attnbank.MergeKVAttention, attnbank/methods/compress/merge_kv.py monograph sec:compress

docs.title: What it changes
docs.text:
Changes the stored context \((\mu, k, v)\) itself. This is the one category that routinely perturbs the integrand, so \(\widehat v \neq v\) and the error has a value term.

It pursues approximation: it is trying to be dense softmax, so it is fair to judge it by output error, and it must supply a correctness anchor saying where it becomes exact.

docs.title: In the paper's notation
docs.text:
sec:compress-merge, prop:compress-merge, prop:error-merge. A partition C_1, ..., C_r of the positions and the map T: x -> cluster(x) define

mu_hat = T_# mu,    mu_hat({i}) = mu(C_i),
y_hat(q) = sum_i mu(C_i) e^{beta <q, k_hat_i>} v_hat_i / sum_i mu(C_i) e^{beta <q, k_hat_i>},

i.e. ToMe's proportional attention: the merged token carries the mu-mass of its preimage, which in log form is the log |C_i| bias. Without it the pushforward is replaced by counting measure on the compressed domain and large clusters are systematically under-weighted.

Expressing it on the original positions. Lift the representatives back, k~_j = k_hat_{T(j)} and v~_j = v_hat_{T(j)}; then pi~_j ∝ e^{beta <q, k~_j>} on the original n positions satisfies pi~ @ v~ = y_hat and sum_j pi~_j = 1. The multiplicity appears automatically, because a cluster of size |C_i| contributes |C_i| identical atoms. That is the sense in which the pushforward is mass-preserving, and it is what tests/test_compress.py checks.

Representatives. k_hat_i and v_hat_i are the within-cluster means. The paper notes this is not the right key representative even for one query: the exact contribution is mu(C_i) exp(Lambda_i(q)) with Lambda_i the log-MGF of the cluster's keys, and by Jensen mean-key merging under-weights every cluster, to leading order by exp(-beta^2 q^T Sigma_i q / 2). The within-cluster covariance is returned in extras so that correction can be studied.

Not causal: clusters span positions on both sides of a query.

Exact limit: n_clusters = None (singleton clusters).

docs.title: Multi-head latent attention
docs.text:
mla · ab.build("mla")

Multi-head latent attention: one joint low-rank KV latent, per-head up-projection.

category compress — one of the seven objects in \(y(q)=\int v\,\mathrm{d}\pi_q\) a method can change objective modify — defines a different operator; fidelity to softmax is not the goal class attnbank.MLAAttention, attnbank/methods/compress/mla.py monograph sec:compress

docs.title: What it changes
docs.text:
Changes the stored context \((\mu, k, v)\) itself. This is the one category that routinely perturbs the integrand, so \(\widehat v \neq v\) and the error has a value term.

It pursues modification: it defines a different operator. Asking how closely it approximates softmax is asking the wrong question — it is not trying to.

docs.title: In the paper's notation
docs.text:
sec:compress-arch. Instead of caching h key–value pairs per position, MLA caches a single latent c_j = W_down [k_j^{(1)}; ...; k_j^{(h)}; v_j^{(1)}; ...] of dimension r, and reconstructs each head's key and value by a per-head up-projection. The cached state per position drops from h (d + d_v) to r.

Like GQA this is an operator modification trained as such; it is in the library for the roofline (it is the other intervention that raises decode arithmetic intensity) and because it is the cleanest example of a compression that couples heads: the latent is shared, so head_independent = False.

The projections are trained in DeepSeek-V2. Here W_down is a fixed seeded Gaussian and the up-projection is its pseudo-inverse, so the reconstruction is the orthogonal projection onto row(W_down). That choice is data-independent, hence causal, and makes the exact limit provable: at r = h (d + d_v) the matrix is square and invertible, the reconstruction is exact, and the operator is dense softmax.

def cost(self, m, n, d, dv, bytes_per_el=2, heads: int = 1):
